chief_complaint: bloody diarrhea, severe eczema, and recurrent ear infections
hpi_details: 12-month-old male presenting with petechiae, bloody diarrhea, and severe intractable eczema covering his face and flexural areas. He has had multiple episodes of otitis media and a recent admission for pneumonia. Initial lab work at an outside hospital showed a very low platelet count and small platelet size.
ideas: parents think his skin condition is causing his infections
concerns: worried about the bleeding in his stool
expectations: wants a strong cream for the eczema and answers about the bleeding

core_concepts: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by the classic triad: Microthrombocytopenia, Eczema, and Recurrent infections.
The defect involves the WAS protein, affecting actin cytoskeleton reorganization in white blood cells and platelets.
Patients have a high risk of developing autoimmune diseases and malignancies (especially lymphoma).
Definitive treatment requires Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT).
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: bloody diarrhea, severe eczema, and recurrent ear infections
Key HPI features: Male infant with classic triad of bleeding/petechiae (due to thrombocytopenia), severe eczema, and recurrent pyogenic infections.
Objective/Exam findings: Petechiae, purpura, severe atopic dermatitis. CBC shows low platelets with uniquely SMALL mean platelet volume (MPV).
common_misconceptions: Misdiagnosing the bleeding as Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP); ITP typically has normal or large platelets, whereas WAS has small platelets.
dangerous_errors: Performing unnecessary splenectomy for presumed ITP without ruling out WAS.
Failing to screen for associated malignancies as the child grows.
management_principles: Supportive care with IVIG, prophylactic antibiotics, and aggressive eczema management.
Refer to Pediatric Immunology/Oncology for HSCT.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 12-month-old male presenting with the triad of bloody diarrhea (petechial bleeding), severe eczema, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections.
reference_soap.objective: Petechiae on extremities. Excoriated erythematous plaques on face/flexures. CBC: Platelets 25k, MPV 5.5 fL (very small).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Admit for evaluation and management of thrombocytopenic bleeding. 2. Platelet transfusion if active severe hemorrhage. 3. Initiate IVIG and prophylactic antibiotics. 4. Topical corticosteroids for eczema. 5. Consult Pediatric Immunology for HSCT planning.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic WATER triad: Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia (micro), Eczema, Recurrent infections
Differentiate WAS thrombocytopenia (small platelets) from ITP (large platelets)
Understand the definitive treatment is stem cell transplant

teaching.one_liner: An X-linked immunodeficiency featuring a triad of small-platelet bleeding, severe eczema, and recurrent infections.
differentials: Severe Atopic Dermatitis with secondary infections
Hyper-IgE Syndrome (eczema and infections, but normal platelets)
red_flags: Unexplained bleeding or petechiae in an infant with eczema
Very low Mean Platelet Volume (MPV) on CBC

must_ask.say: Have you noticed any tiny red or purple spots on his skin, or unexplained bruising?
Has his skin rash been difficult to control with regular creams?
Does he get sick with fevers or ear infections more often than other babies his age?

history.answer: My baby has had blood-streaked diarrhea for three days, and his skin rash has become completely uncontrollable.
The blood is bright red, mixed right in with brownish watery stool rather than looking dark or tarry.
It looks like bloody mucus smeared in his diaper and mixed throughout the runny stool.
It started three days ago, and he has four or five loose diapers a day with a couple of teaspoons of bloody stool each time.
He does not cry or show discomfort when he passes stool, so his bottom does not seem painful.
I have checked his bottom and have not noticed any bumps, piles, or tears around his opening.
He has not been constipated at all; his stools have been entirely loose and watery.
His bowel movements were usually soft and once a day, but this sudden frequent diarrhea began three days ago.
He gets fussy because his skin itches so much, but he does not pull his legs up or act like he has belly cramps.
He has loose watery stools with slimy mucus, but he has not run any fever this week.
He looks slightly pale, but he is awake, interacts with us, and has not fainted or seemed limp.
His appetite has dropped a little over the past two days, and his weight gain has been sluggish over the past few months.
He has not vomited at all, and he has never thrown up blood or dark fluid.
He has never looked yellow, and he has no history of jaundice or liver disease.
We have never given him aspirin, ibuprofen, blood thinners, or iron drops.
He has not eaten any beets, blueberries, or anything with dark artificial food coloring.
He has never had a scope exam, and no one in our family has had colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.
He gets tiny pinpoint red spots on his shins and bruises very easily even with gentle handling.
He has had severe, intensely itchy, scaly eczema across his face, neck, and elbow folds since he was two months old that never clears up.
He has had four separate ear infections this past year, and he had to be hospitalized for pneumonia two months ago.
We thought maybe all these open scratches from his severe eczema were letting germs into his body and causing his infections.
We are terrified seeing blood in his diaper and don't understand why he bleeds and bruises so easily.
We want a stronger prescription cream to give him relief from this rash, and we need clear answers about why he is bleeding.
He was diagnosed with severe infant eczema at two months, followed by frequent middle ear infections and one round of pneumonia.
He was admitted to the pediatric ward for four days for pneumonia two months ago, but he has never had surgery.
We apply one percent hydrocortisone cream to his rash twice a day, and he has not taken any other regular medications.
He has no known allergies to any medicines, formulas, or foods.
My mother told me that her brother passed away in infancy from a severe bleeding complication, but my husband and I are healthy.
He was born at full term without complications, but his umbilical cord stump kept oozing blood for several days before falling off.
He has received all his scheduled baby vaccinations on time, though his weight has fallen toward the fifteenth percentile.
He stays at home with me, has not attended daycare, and nobody smokes around our home.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 90/58 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, irritable 12-month-old male infant actively scratching his cheeks and arms, with mild pallor and no acute respiratory distress.
Mildly pale palpebral conjunctivae bilaterally; sclerae are clear and anicteric without petechiae or jaundice.
Bilateral tympanic membranes are dull and mildly thickened with reduced light reflexes, but no acute bulging, erythema, or purulent drainage.
Bilateral lung fields are clear to auscultation with equal air entry and no wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs audible.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without visible distension, caput medusae, or surgical scars.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended in all four quadrants with no involuntary guarding or rigidity.
Liver edge is soft and palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, and spleen tip is palpable 1 cm below the left costal margin without tenderness.
Perianal inspection reveals normal skin and anatomy without fissures, hemorrhoidal tissue, skin tags, or perianal fistula.
Normal sphincter tone with an empty rectal vault and no masses; gross brown liquid stool with visible streaks of red blood noted on the glove.
Widespread erythematous, excoriated, and lichenified eczema plaques on face, neck, and flexural folds, accompanied by scattered petechiae and small purpuric lesions on the lower limbs.
Small, shotty, mobile, non-tender lymph nodes measuring less than 1 centimeter palpable in bilateral cervical and inguinal chains.
